I'm also curious if this is intended as a general move or only something specific to conversation.h and request response tracking.

In short: I think most of the READMEs should be migrated to Doxygen or the WSDG, as appropriate. Longer response below:

Warning, rant incoming. It's possible some of these opinions are flat out wrong, so please feel free to speak up correct me:

1. Wireshark's documentation is spread across many locations: README's, Wiki pages, WSUG/WSDG, and the source code itself. This makes finding the relevant documentation difficult.
1. Wireshark's header files are barely documented - when I ran `coverxygen` in https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/issues/17758 it came in at about 1% coverage. This makes it harder to understand function parameters and what functions do.
1. The combination of the documentation being spread out and functions not being well-documented makes it harder for new developers to work with or contribute to Wireshark. It also means that that development heavily relies on the people with the institutional knowledge

The solutions to me seem fairly straightforward (at least in theory; implementation is always harder):
1. Consolidate knowledge as much as possible so there are fewer locations to search and that it's closer to the ground truth, so it doesn't have to be maintained as a separate entity. In my opinion, this means migrating as much of the wiki content and README files into either the WSUG/WSDG or the source code. I think that the WSDG is best suited for explaining the larger project and its concepts. However, anything related to how the code works or is intended to be used is best placed inside the source code documentation, as that's the closest place as to where it would need to be referenced.
1. Make code documentation a first-class feature. Link to the Doxygen code on the homepage. In the pre-checks, mandate that new code be documented. Make a focused effort to document existing code. Not every function needs to be documented, but I think a good goal for v4.0 would be to aim to fully document all header files used by dissectors. A rough check indicates there were about 107 unique headers imported from epan that were not in the dissectors directory ( Calculated by running `wireshark/epan/dissectors$ egrep "include <([^<]+)>" . -r | cut -d" " -f2 | cut -d"        " -f1 | sort | uniq | grep -v "dissector" | grep -v packet- | wc` ). This would help lower the reliance on existing institutional knowledge and make it easier for new developers to become productive faster.

> Wireshark's documentation is spread across many locations: README's, Wiki pages, WSUG/WSDG, and the source code itself. This makes finding the relevant documentation difficult.

+1

> However, anything related to how the code works or is intended to be used is best placed inside the source code documentation, as that's the closest place as to where it would need to be referenced.

So where would the Doxygen documentation appear?  It sounds as if it would be a separate document from the WSDG, which might be the "Wireshark API Reference"  or "Wireshark Developer Reference" separate from the "Wireshark Developer's Guide".
They are published here: https://www.wireshark.org/docs/wsar_html/index.html

Doxygen is OK to annotate C code. Moving README.request_response_tracking seems approriate as it is short and mostly deals with a single API. For anything more elaborate I'm not convinced of its value.

I also don't recognize much of a documentation usability problem. it can always be better and it is a bit spread out but I do not see this as a significant barrier. I personally would prefer to invest more effort on improving the WSUG/WSDG.

> I personally would prefer to invest more effort on improving the WSUG/WSDG.
